reading.body:
AI's training data problem now has ten separately named insurance lines, which means the legal risk of building models is being priced line by line rather than as one exposure.

The ten items divide by where the risk enters. Four concern inputs: scraping copyrighted training data, harvesting personal data without consent, source code leaking into a public training set, and collection that is lawful in the model's home country but unlawful where the data originates. Three concern outputs: generated material that infringes a patent, unauthorised voice or likeness, and provenance or watermarking tools that fail to stop synthetic media. Two concern the contract rather than the conduct: whether hyperscaler IP indemnities hold up against their own policy conditions, and whether commercial use breaches a non-commercial clause in an open weight licence. The tenth, performance collapse from training on synthetic data carrying hidden errors, is not an intellectual property risk at all.

That last item is the tell. A category built around copyright and patents has absorbed a model quality failure, which suggests training data exposure is being underwritten as one bundle rather than as clean legal categories. For AI specifically, the list is a forecast of where liability is expected to land. Hyperscaler indemnification appears as its own line rather than as a settled matter, which says the guarantees are not treated as sufficient on their own. The cross-border item says the same collection can be lawful and unlawful at once, a problem no single policy resolves.

What this does not cover matters as much. There are no premiums, no policy limits, no claim counts, and no indication of which of the ten are actually written. A taxonomy of coverage is evidence of what insurers think could go wrong, not evidence of what has. Nothing here concerns compute, buildings, or power, so the physical constraints on AI scaling sit outside this data entirely.
